articles.title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
articles.text:
The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.

In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.

And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.

The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".

Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".

Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?

This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.

This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry.

However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced.

No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports.

Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape.

In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market.

But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports.

The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040.

Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation.

The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes.

The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale.

Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people".

Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year.

A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal.

This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments.

The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own calculations.

Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions.

The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off.

There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents.

The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere.

Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals.

The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market.

The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.

articles.title: Tinned food and long-life milk boost retail sales after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
articles.text:
Retail sales rose in October, driven by people buying long-life food such as tinned goods and UHT milk, according to official figures.

Sales volumes were 0.7% higher as people responded to the government's emergency preparedness "Be Ready" campaign, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.

The campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.

Separate research released last week suggested that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying.

The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days' worth of food and water in their homes.

Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.

Data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator indicated last week that people were stocking up on items including tinned meat, bottled water and hand sanitiser.

The latest official sales figures, external from the ONS add to the evidence that the public has begun stockpiling.

"Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government's 'Be Ready' campaign," ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said.

"Meanwhile fuel sales have been recovering from earlier low levels, despite pump prices rising again."

The rise in retail sales last month beat some economists' expectations - they had predicted a slight fall - and the increase came after a 0.6% decline in September.

As well as sales being boosted by people buying essentials, visits to art galleries and clothing purchases were also higher in October.

articles.title: Fish and eggs al desko? The dos and don'ts of lunch at work
articles.text:
There are two types of office workers: those who eat lunch al-desko, and those who have to endure the smell of everyone else's.

Few things are more likely to test workplace relationships than the person sitting next to you proudly unveiling a container of reheated fish.

From tuna sandwiches and boiled eggs to crumbly and sticky treats that leave a mess on the keyboard, what is considered OK to eat in the office can be surprisingly divisive.

"We all know not to bring in a microwave fish pie, that is the law," says civil servant Sarah.

She admits she has, in fact, committed the offence herself in a previous workplace and jokes "that's the reason I left".

But fish isn't the only food causing office friction and Casey says his regular snack of cinnamon pretzels has been causing "quite a bit of havoc".

"The sugar's going everywhere and it's getting in my laptop keys," he admits. No-one in the office has commented on it yet but he says he's hiding the crumbs by "shuffling them off the desk".

Boiled eggs also split opinion. Laura, who works in finance, says she's been teased by colleagues for eating them.

"In my defence, it was high protein, it was cost-effective and healthy – I swear by a good boiled egg."

She thinks that no food is off limits at the desk. "Coming from an Asian background where you'd eat fish for breakfast I am very open to it being eaten."

Ashlea Fisher, who runs her own recruitment company, has tackled the issue of smelly food in the office head on when she asked a member of staff to stop bringing in fish after "the smell was so bad that a pregnant colleague was feeling physically sick".

"I'm a big believer in being able to have an honest conversation with your team," she says, and suggests that other people in her position should approach a conversation lightly and be conscious of not embarrassing colleagues.

"Nobody should feel judged for what they eat, and we should respect different cultures and dietary requirements, but being mindful of the people around you is simply good workplace etiquette."

Laura, whose working day can occasionally finish at 2am, says stepping away from her desk is a non-negotiable and she makes a point of taking an hour for lunch, describing it as "essential for maintaining my sanity".

"I take my lunch break as much as possible, for the sake of my eyes and mental wellbeing," she says.

But others are less precious about it. Content creator Manny says he has lunch at his desk "most of the time".

His work is task-based and his company operates a policy of "do the work when you want to do it".

"Usually you just take 20 minutes to eat something, but on another day you might take an hour. You just kind of feel it out," he says.

articles.title: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
articles.text:
New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force.

Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason.

Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all".

But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers.

The new Airbnb rules, announced last month, allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed.

Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities.

Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts, external "who need to take action" it said.

Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it.

If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks".

Airbnb said chores can make customers hesitate about booking through the platform, arguing that making house rules "clearer" would increase the number of clients.

But some hosts have said they may have to pass the extra cleaning costs on to guests.

Lisa Clewes, who runs a Welsh holiday let, told the BBC she was "horrified" at the state her guests left the house after a dinner party.

There were broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden.

Clewes said it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property.

She said guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her customers.

articles.title: Mouldy, infested housing for vulnerable people sold as ethical investments abroad
articles.text:
"This building is hell on Earth," says Phil, describing the black mould and rats at Castleview House, the block of flats in Runcorn, Cheshire, where he lives.

But to an estate agent called Britské Reality - which translates as British Real Estate - working with investors hundreds of miles away in the Czech Republic, the flat Phil rents through his benefits was an exciting business opportunity.

The estate agent's marketing material said the flat was a government-funded source of income for investors, where tenants were taken care of and the property was in excellent condition.

A Czech investor bought it last year for £163,150, more than double the £75,000 cost of similar apartments in the block.

The BBC has found more than 40 companies marketing similar properties to individuals in the UK and abroad, as businesses seek to profit from a government system intended to provide housing and support for vulnerable people.

About a dozen of these companies work with a property developer called Lee Jones, whose company sold Phil's flat.

The homes they are selling to investors are advertised as supported accommodation, a type of housing for people with issues including mental health problems or drug abuse issues, as well as people fleeing domestic violence.

Providers offering what is known as supported exempt accommodation are allowed to charge the taxpayer more than the usual housing benefit cap, because they have higher running costs. Tenants are entitled to care, support and supervision - although how much support should be provided is not defined.

While there are legitimate providers helping people back into independent living, the BBC has previously reported on how some are exploiting the system by taking the higher housing benefit payments but failing to provide support.

Our latest investigation found companies marketing supported housing properties to people in Hong Kong, Macau, Nigeria, Turkey, the Netherlands, the UK and other countries as a "secure", "government-backed" investment.

We also found adverts made misleading promises about the quality of the accommodation and support, with tenants saying they were receiving little or no care, while we observed examples of poor quality, unsafe accommodation.

Housing charities and experts have told the BBC the sector has been transformed into a profit-generating machine at the expense of some tenants' safety, care, and dignity.

Labour MP Abena Oppong-Asare, who chairs the Housing Select Committee, said it was "outrageous" that supported housing properties were being marketed as investments "particularly where there's public funds involved".

The BBC's findings were "alarming" and showed a sector "open to abuse", she added.

Lee Jones's company The Investment Room converted Castleview House in 2019 from an office block into more than 200 residential flats, including the one where Phil now lives.

Then Jones partnered with Nurture Housing Association. His company granted Nurture a 25-year-lease on some of the flats, to provide housing for people on government benefits. Jones has a close business relationship with Nurture's chief executive Chris Smith, with the pair also acting as joint directors of other housing companies.

Jones then worked with estate agents, which marketed the housing to investors in the UK and overseas using the regular cashflow generated by the 25-year lease with Nurture and the promise of government funding to justify inflated prices.

Lee Jones and Nurture have repeated this with property developments across England, including in Doncaster, Rotherham, Stockton-on-Tees and Bradford. These type of properties are also in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland but are funded and regulated differently.

Because neither profit-making private companies nor individuals can act as supported housing providers themselves, co-operation between developers, investors and publicly funded providers has become common.

The Czech marketing material found by the BBC said Nurture provides housing for people with mental health issues who receive the "aftercare program pursuant to Section 117 of the Mental Health Act", meaning they have been sectioned and discharged from hospital with a detailed care plan.

But Phil says he has never been sectioned under the Mental Health Act.

He does have severe depression and anxiety, and he is currently out of work. But he says he has never had any support or care, or met anyone working for Nurture during his time at the flat.

"Whoever marketed this property, the way they've worded it is total dishonesty," says Phil. "If they're looking to make as much profit as they can, then they clearly have no plans to fix the issues in the building."

Phil had no idea the flat he rents had been sold to overseas investors in May 2025 until the BBC contacted him. But there were clues: bills addressed to someone called Jan Hála had been coming through the letterbox for months.

Lee Jones told us that the properties his companies provide are "good quality accommodation" and he has no responsibility for the communal areas of Castleview House since he sold the freehold in 2021. He denied his relationship with Chris Smith amounted to a conflict of interest, but did not respond to questions about his role in marketing the properties.

Jan Hála, the Czech investor who now owns Phil's flat, and the Britské Reality estate agency did not respond to requests for comment.

We spoke to several other people living in flats run by Nurture Housing Association in Castleview House who said they were in supported accommodation. They reported receiving little or no help from Nurture but were afraid to speak out publicly for fear of eviction and becoming homeless.

There is also evidence that marketing materials for investors buying flats in Castleview were misleading. Investors were told Nurture was providing "specialist supported housing" - a claim which is repeated on its website.

According to the Regulator of Social Housing, this would mean it was providing a high level of care, equivalent to living in a care home.

But Nurture had not been registered as a specialised supported housing provider, the regulator said, and its claim to be providing this was "shocking".

In a statement, Nurture acknowledged that Castleview House is managed under a "general housing management model" and does not form part of its supported housing portfolio. It said it provided supported housing elsewhere through partners which were registered providers.

It said the Czech advert found by the BBC related to "historic marketing material" produced by third parties.

However, the BBC has seen marketing material from several other agents selling flats in Castleview House to investors, which also claim that Nurture is providing supported housing to the residents on a 25-year lease.

Nurture said it is not directly involved with the companies marketing the properties. But it said: "We will be reviewing communications with relevant agents and reminding them of the importance of ensuring that any information relating to Nurture is accurate, transparent and does not create misunderstanding regarding the accommodation or services provided."

While there are doubts about what kind of housing Nurture has been providing, the BBC also found other flats sold to investors overseas with tenants who were in supported exempt accommodation.

The web of companies involved in providing this housing and cross-border ownership means it can be difficult for vulnerable tenants to get help when there are problems with properties.

"The way that the current system works is there's different levels of involvement by different organisations and companies and no-one is directly accountable," Abena Oppong-Asare, the housing committee chairwoman, told us.

Mo, who has mental health issues, was housed in a studio flat in Cricklewood, north London, after he became homeless. The converted house containing his flat was bought by Gemelli London 2 Limited, a company run by French nationals living in the Czech Republic, for £1.83m in January last year.

He says his supported housing provider, Windrush Alliance, receives nearly £2,000 a month via Barnet Council for the flat. Mo says he receives £340 in universal credit for living expenses every month - but he is expected to pay Windrush a monthly £120 service charge out of that.

Last year his ceiling collapsed after a leak went unrepaired for more than a year and Mo was temporarily housed in another flat in the property.

Mo says his weekly visits from a Windrush support worker feel like a tick-box exercise and do not help him with the mental health issues which have been keeping him out of work.

Gemelli's director Stephane Boussier told the BBC that when the company bought the property "no complaints from residents were disclosed". It was made aware of issues in August 2025, he said, and since then has "raised them with Windrush in writing, inspected the property and pressed for them to be resolved".

He added that Gemelli London 2 Limited receives about £1,365 per flat per month from Windrush and does not receive any of the extra housing benefit that would be used for vulnerable tenants.

Windrush said it was aware of issues at Mo's property and was "working with the building owner to put them right". According to Gemelli, the ceiling was repaired after the BBC contacted the two companies.

Windrush has previously been criticised by the Regulator for Social Housing for a "failure to meet the standards" of the regulator, including failing to ensure "tenants are safe in their homes".

It acknowledged that it "fell short in the past". It wrote off £1.8m in "funds to former directors and companies under their control", saying the company's financial position had been "compromised" by their actions. The company now has a new board in place.

Windrush told us its "priority is residents, not investors" and the rates it charges "are agreed with the relevant local authorities" and "any surplus is reinvested in our homes and services".

In Bradford, the BBC visited City Exchange and Colonnade House, two former office blocks which Lee Jones has converted into housing - with Nurture Housing Association managing many of the flats.

Many of the properties there were advertised as supported housing investments. Residents showed us cockroach infestations, faulty fire alarms, broken lifts, leaks through the ceiling and black mould.

Nurture Housing said it was only responsible for the individual homes that it manages and does not manage communal areas or "wider building infrastructure".

"Nurture Housing and its managing agents regularly raise these concerns with the block manager," the company said.

The freeholder for Phil's block, Castleview House, and City Exchange, blamed "defects" by the developer Lee Jones for the problems with the buildings and said it was taking legal action. Colonnade House has had several building management companies in recent years and the latest said it was addressing the problems.

None of these companies or individuals are breaking the law, but critics say they are exploiting a lack of regulation in the sector.

Three years after the Supported Housing Act was passed in England, which would put in place a licensing regime for supported housing providers and give local councils more powers to shut down providers that failed to meet the standards, it still has not been implemented.

"It's taken too long," said Jasmine Basran, head of policy and campaigns at housing charity Crisis. "In the meantime, this an area where we've seen the worst kind of exploitation."

Additional reporting by Lorna Acquah and Abi Smitton

articles.title: Anthropic becomes one of world's most valuable public companies in first-of-its kind IPO
articles.text:
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion (£1.34 trillion).

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.

Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 each, showing there was plenty of excitement around AI.

Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?

In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.53, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day as the shares closed at $97.17.

Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet, which was down by 2.9%, while Amazon lost almost 3.9%.

The buildout happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.

The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.

"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."

While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.

The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet more quickly.

It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.

As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.

The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.

That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.

Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.

Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.

But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.

With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.

"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.

So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth more than $1.7 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.

"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."

A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.

One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.

Such regulation is currently unlikely at the federal level. US President Donald Trump on Thursday spoke about AI during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China, alongside Chinese and Russian counterparts, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Trump reiterated his position against "any form of robust regulation" around the technology, adding, "we won't allow that to happen, frankly."

The same day, however, a bipartisan group of US lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.

A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.

Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.

Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".

"AI carries real risks," she added.

Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

articles.title: Anthropic may have solved major maths problem Reimann hypothesis
articles.text:
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.

Levent Alpöge said, external on Friday, a day after Anthropic made its US stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.

If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".

The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.

As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.

It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.

Named after the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.

Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.

Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.

"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."

"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.

The complete textual proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.

Terence Tao, a prominent mathematician, said on Friday, external that verification of the proof is still some way off.

"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.

No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.

OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools were able to solve part of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.

More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.

The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.

Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions in maths, external and physics, external.

A group of maths scholars said, external AI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".

"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.

A month later, OpenAI released, external what it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.

It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

articles.title: Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut
articles.text:
Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (£62bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the loss-making business meant more stock was sold than originally planned. Anthropic's shares have been priced at $83, up from the proposed $70-$78 range.

Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion.

The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for fast-growing AI sector. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to publicly sell its shares.

Vast amounts of money have been poured into AI infrastructure and the development of AI based tools. But questions are being raised over whether and when those investments will pay off.

The seven founders, who set up Anthropic up in 2021, will become multi-billionaires immediately.

The company's $1.5tn estimated valuation is on a "diluted" basis, a broader reflection of the firm's value that takes things like employee stock options into account. On a basic share count Anthropic is worth about $1.1tn, more valuable than Walmart and Samsung but less than Tesla and Meta.

But strong demand could push its share price, and overall valuation, higher, once shares are publicly traded.

One early investor in the company who spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymity, said the original sale was heavily oversubscribed, with demand ten times the number of shares available.

Anthropic's revenues have ballooned in the last year, to $33bn in the nine months to September this year, as the market for its tools, designed to speed up processes including coding, writing and digesting information, has grown.

But net losses have also increased, reaching $104bn for the same period, according to the company's IPO document.

Leah Bramwell from Canaccord Wealth said there had been strong interest in Anthropic shares "across the board" including both institutional and retail - that is private individual - investors, which she said suggested it was not simply a "retail-driven frenzy into into AI names".

In total Anthropic could raise $107bn. Over $81bn comes from the public share sale, with an additional $26bn from separate investments from a group of tech firms including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.

Anthropic could raise a further $12bn through an additional provision, which is normal practice, to permit further shares to be sold if demand is very high.

Elon Musk's SpaceX raised an initial $75bn in its IPO in June this year.

The company soared in value when it joined the Nasdaq, reaching $2.2tn, although in the weeks that followed, the share price fell.

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year. Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology.

While there is excitement around Anthropic's listing, there is also some concern from investors about its future ability to generate profits in a competitive area.

Yang Wang, a principle analyst at Counterpoint Research, said the central issue was whether it could "keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.

However, the share sale would give investors "direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity", Wang said.

Technology stocks have lost value in recent weeks following the US midterm elections. Democrats, who now control of both chambers of Congress, are expected to be tougher on AI regulation. Some Democrat candidates opposed the rapid build of data centres required to run AI.

But Anthropic went ahead with its market listing, despite the market volatility, because it needed to tap into additional funds, said Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower.

"AI is financially demanding," Norton told the BBC. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more and so the time has come."

Broader anxieties about the AI industry remain.

Competition from low-cost rival models is growing.

Expensive computer chips, necessary for the industry to operate, are in short supply.

And the US Federal Reserve is concerned about high AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss interest rates, as well as the high concentration of AI exposure among a small number of firms.

With additional reporting by Rachel Clun

articles.title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading
articles.text:
As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory.

Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by 9% on Friday, ceding most of the gains from the biggest initial public offering in history. They dropped to $88.30, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.

Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.

US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. Nvidia fell 14%, eliminating hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap.

Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”

Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.

European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.

The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO.

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.

“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.

Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI buildout.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”

Nvidia shares fell byafter California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.

Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.

Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

articles.title: Judge approves $7.25bn Bayer payout to settle claims that Roundup causes cancer
articles.text:
A Missouri judge on Friday approved Bayer’s $7.25bn settlement of lawsuits ⁠alleging that its weedkiller ​Roundup causes cancer, potentially resolving litigation that has weighed on the German company for close to a decade.

Judge Timothy Boyer of a state court in St Louis ⁠found the settlement “fair, reasonable and adequate”.

He overruled objections that payouts to individual cancer victims would be too low because claimants who previously settled were paid more.

The judge also said delaying payouts could ⁠force victims, including those whose cancer is terminal, to wait “an indeterminate number of years” to be paid.

Bayer had faced approximately ​65,000 claims in US state and federal courts from ‌people who said they developed cancer ‌after using Roundup at home or on the job.

The settlement announced in February aimed to resolve nearly all current ‌and future Roundup claims in the US.

“The court’s final approval is a decisive milestone in the company’s strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation,” Bayer’s CEO, Bill Anderson, said in a statement.

Bayer has faced extensive litigation over Roundup, and had seen its share price fall 46% since it bought Monsanto, which produces the weedkiller, for $63bn in 2018.

The company settled much of the Roundup litigation for $10.9bn in 2020, ‌but was unable to win court approval of a $1.25bn settlement to resolve future Roundup claims.

Bayer has long maintained that Roundup and its active ingredient glyphosate were safe, and that decades ​of studies had shown that glyphosate did not cause cancer.

The settlement was approved five months after the US supreme court overturned a $1.25m jury award for a Missouri man, John Durnell, who blamed years of exposure to glyphosate in Roundup for his non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

In a 7-2 decision, the court agreed with Bayer that a federal law regulating pesticides barred failure-to-warn claims brought under ⁠state law, undercutting a central pillar of many lawsuits.

Christopher Seeger, a lawyer for ​many of the plaintiffs, said the Durnell ​decision narrowed the ability of Roundup victims ​to pursue claims in court.

“We look forward to getting this relief into the hands of all ​Roundup victims as quickly ‌as possible,” he ​said in a statement.

Lawyers for ​some of the Roundup victims who objected to the settlement did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The settlement excludes some lawsuits that remain pending in federal court. Bayer has said that about 200 of those cases were still being litigated, and that the supreme court decision gave it strong defenses.

articles.title: Chelsea: Leeds penalty call reopens Premier League handball debate
articles.text:
It is rare when a key handball decision is given for the widespread response to be "that is correct".

Often the discussion centres on the desire for a seemingly more lenient interpretation taking into account perceived intent.

And that is again a talking point after the crucial penalty given against Chelsea in Saturday's 4-1 home defeat by Leeds which ended up putting the visitors ahead for the first time.

Interestingly, despite the perception, handball penalties are much rarer in the Premier League compared with the other top five leagues in Europe.

Last season, there were 22 penalties for handball in the English top flight's 380 games - easily the lowest tally.

Spain's La Liga (36) and Italy's Serie A (38) produced the most.

This season in the Premier League there have been three in 106 matches - less than in 2025-26.

So why was the penalty given against Chelsea's Morgan Rogers?

The feeling among Premier League clubs is that handball is in a good place now, where the arm must either be fully extended away from the body, raised, or be a deliberate act to be punishable.

And it is the last of these that applied to the penalty given against Rogers, which to some might seem a bit harsh, considering the Premier League's more relaxed interpretation of handball.

There are, however, a few key reasons why referee Michael Oliver pointed to the spot, why the video assistant referee (VAR) did not intervene, and why it will be judged as a correct decision.

Two of the factors which a referee looks for when judging a potential handball apply here.

First, how far the ball travelled.

As Jayden Bogle's shot was from distance, a defender is considered to have more time to adjust their body and react - and thus avoid a potential handball.

Most important in this case is the movement of the arm.

When Bogle shoots, Rogers' arm is not raised - but it comes up to the flight of the ball.

Crucially, had Rogers kept his arm in its original position - lower and level with his midriff - there would not have been a handball offence.

What does this mean? Put simply, if the ball would have hit the body if it had not come off the arm, it is considered to have no impact.

But this case was different. Rogers raised his arm and that is what led to the ball being deflected away. This is considered a deliberate act, and this trumps all other considerations.

Perhaps there was a question about whether the ball hit Rogers too high on his arm, and thus should not be a handball offence.

It was close, but it looked like it was in what the laws call the 'red zone', the part of the arm which is punishable for handball.

But this really would be the only reason the VAR, Michael Salisbury, would have any cause to consider an on-field review.

We saw a similar case last season, in terms of how this kind of handball offence is judged - coincidentally involving a penalty awarded to Leeds.

As Anton Stach's powerful strike arrowed towards goal, Everton defender James Tarkowski leaned to his left in an attempt to block the shot - and did so with his arm, which was tucked tightly to the side of his body.

Everton manager David Moyes described the decision as "wrong", but it was absolutely correct in law.

That Tarkowski's arm was close to his side was irrelevant because of the deliberate act of leaning into the path of the ball.

Likewise, Rogers raised his arm to stop the ball and a penalty was a justifiable call.

Despite the Premier League having a more lenient interpretation of the handball law already, it is clear that many observers would like it to go further.

For example, BBC Match of the Day pundit Alan Shearer echoed many when he said there should be more intent for a handball.

"I didn't agree with the penalty when Michael Oliver gave it," he said.

"I know once the on-field decision is made there is a high bar to review it, but I don't think officials are allowed to use common sense.

"Morgan Rogers is not deliberately trying to stop the ball. He just doesn't want it hitting him in the face.

"Although the penalty came at an important point in the match, Chelsea were deservedly beaten by a much stronger, far more physical and better-organised Leeds team."

Rogers may argue he raised his arm to protect his face.

This is one of the possible mitigating factors, but usually only applies when a player raises their hands to their face - not using the arm as a barrier.

Chelsea boss Xabi Alonso said that, while he did not "want to make a big thing about it", the penalty should not have been awarded.

"For me it was quite a harsh decision," he told Sky Sports. "I would not have given a penalty. I don't want to make a big thing about it but for me it's not a penalty."

articles.title: ATP Finals: Carlos Alcaraz battles back against Ben Shelton to reach final
articles.text:
Carlos Alcaraz will have the chance to end his wait for a first ATP Finals title after completing a superb comeback victory over Ben Shelton.

The indomitable Spaniard recovered from a flat start to outlast Shelton 3-6 6-3 7-6 (7-1) and secure a return to the showpiece, 12 months after losing to Jannik Sinner.

Alcaraz again competed with strapping around his upper-left leg having injured his hamstring earlier this week, but produced his best tennis when it mattered most.

After extending his winning streak to 13 matches, the seven-time major winner will face world number one Alexander Zverev or Daniil Medvedev in Sunday's final.

Asked how he was feeling physically, with little over 24 hours to recover for that match, Alcaraz said: "Today was a really important test. I think it went great.

"I'm probably not pushing myself to the limit. Without this problem in my leg I could move differently, probably even harder.

"But I'm realising that I just need to be careful with it and sometimes I don't have to push myself to the limit, I don't have to run for every ball."

Alcaraz is through to his seventh final of 2026, a total unmatched by any men's singles player despite his four-month absence with a wrist injury.

The 23-year-old has been in scintillating form since his return to action at the US Open, which concluded in a quarter-final epic against Shelton in September.

He has now won 20 of his past 21 matches, sweeping back-to-back titles at the Vienna Open and Paris Masters prior to this tournament - including taking revenge on Shelton to triumph at the latter.

"I think this rivalry is just getting better and better. It's going to be a great match-up in the future," the third-ranked Alcaraz said after another close match against the world number four.

"Every time we face each other, it's a great battle. It is one of those matches that makes me be a better player and gives me a lot of feedback about what I have to improve."

Victory over Alcaraz in New York marked the biggest win of the 24-year-old Shelton's career, and a repeat of that result appeared within his grasp.

While the hamstring injury Alcaraz sustained earlier this week did not prevent him winning every set in a perfect group campaign, the Australian Open winner was second-best in a subdued start.

articles.title: Manchester City 1-1 Fulham: Elliot Anderson and Ayyoub Bouaddi leave Enzo Maresca with Enzo Fernandez dilemma
articles.text:
There may have been some eyebrows raised before kick-off when Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca decided to drop club record signing Enzo Fernandez to the bench against Fulham.

Fernandez's lengthy excursions back home to Argentina for their two fixtures during the international break may have been a factor in Maresca's thinking when selecting his starting XI for this game.

If it was, the Italian refrained from giving that as a reason. "I just think for this game it's better having Ayyoub Bouaddi in there," he told TNT Sports shortly before kick-off.

Even so, the move was a significant one as his side were in desperate need of victory after suffering three straight Premier League defeats. That winless streak extended to four after being held to a 1-1 draw.

Maresca had an opportunity to fix the issues in his set-up during the two-week break and admitted on Friday he was searching for "more balance" in the "defensive line, midfield and up front".

The pairing of the steady Bouaddi and all-action Elliot Anderson in the centre of the park was the crucial call, and it may have given Maresca some idea as to how to approach the forthcoming run of games.

"Ayyoub with Elliot were both really good," said Maresca. "Today we used Elliot a bit more attacking midfielder, he arrived inside the box and scored a fantastic goal, he had three or four moments around the box where he was really dangerous.

"It is another solution for us. In this moment, we are trying to know each other more as players and also to find the right solution."

Loud jeers greeted the full-time whistle at Etihad Stadium, a culmination of the feeling that was brewing from the home supporters throughout the game.

There was a nervous tension from the beginning, which seemed to seep on to the players on the pitch.

City displayed a flat first-half performance in which they fell behind courtesy of Rodrigo Muniz's superb curling effort, and they needed a stunning second-half volley from Anderson to rescue a point.

The England international is restricted to sitting in front of the back four when Fernandez is in the side, but has the licence to roam when Bouaddi is deployed beside him.

Aside from scoring a spectacular first Premier League goal for City, Anderson created a match-high three chances and had a 100% success rate from 16 passes in the final third of the pitch.

He also had more touches in the opposition box (7), contested more duels than any other player (17) and no-one else managed to win possession back more times than him.

After dragging his side level, another marauding run into the box was snuffed out by the visiting defenders before Rayan Cherki was brought on, which meant Anderson had to retreat back down the pitch.

Maresca needed to change things in order to apply some fresh impetus in the attacking third, but the substitution of Cherki for Phil Foden seemed to limit Anderson's capabilities.

"It's not a good result, especially off the back of three losses," former City goalkeeper Joe Hart told BBC Sport. "There was some good stuff in there.

"It felt like Elliot Anderson was going to take the game by the scruff of the neck but then Cherki came on and took his position. So he [Anderson] didn't have as much of an impact on the game.

"I understood the change - when the lines are deep, there were chances of Cherki unlocking Fulham, but they just defended so well and they also offered a threat on the break."

City overhauled their midfield to the tune of £327m with the signings of trio Fernandez, Anderson and Bouaddi.

The £125m club record acquisition Fernandez had made the 14,000-mile round-trip from Manchester to Buenos Aires for Argentina's friendlies against Uruguay and Costa Rica.

The trip allowed him to take the opportunity to pay a visit to boyhood club River Plate, but it is at his current club where there are question marks as to how he fits into the side.

Bouaddi's presence provides more insurance in front of the defence and the 19-year-old Moroccan has the ability to keep the ball ticking.

It means Anderson can play his natural game - but where, then, does Fernandez fit in?

The number 10 position tends to be occupied by either Cherki or Foden, while Maresca pointed out in his pre-match news conference that City "won games with Enzo and lost games with Enzo".

But the manager clearly has to work out how to get the best out of Fernandez, who was given the final five minutes against Fulham in place of Bouaddi.

"There is no point in having a brilliant squad like Manchester City if you are not going to take that into account," said Hart.

"It's very much understandable, if you're going to have a squad and you trust everyone - if someone's done the travelling, he has done the game time, you have got to expect to not use him as much."

City host Napoli in the Champions League on Tuesday followed by a huge trip to Arsenal next Sunday, knowing they could head to the Emirates eight points behind the champions.

Maresca added: "For sure we don't like these kind of moments in terms of four games in a row without a win

"We also know that, unfortunately, it is normal or part of the path, you go through these kind of moments. It is important that we find a way to keep clean sheets that sometimes you need to win games 1-0 for a small difference."

Mikel Arteta's men know all about that and City now need to take a leaf out of their book.

articles.title: Wales v Australia: Welsh heroes aim to back up historic All Blacks win
articles.text:
The Australia fixture was meant to be Wales' big shot.

It was the chance to finally claim the scalp of a southern hemisphere big gun. The opportunity to make a statement ahead of the 2027 World Cup that they are capable of beating any of the top teams on their day.

But Steve Tandy's side went seven days early.

Wales will now attempt to claim a hat-trick of Cardiff wins in the Nations Championship on Saturday night after the most unlikely of victories against New Zealand.

It is a success that has changed the November narrative. Rather than "can they do it?", the question is now "can they back it up?".

Wales' win against the All Blacks was arguably the biggest shock in international rugby since Japan beat South Africa in Brighton in the 2015 World Cup.

What is rarely mentioned is that the Brave Blossoms - hindered by a farcical four-day turnaround - failed to back that up when thumped by Scotland in Gloucester in their following game.

Japan caused another surprise on home soil in 2019 when they beat Ireland and that time they did follow up with victories against Samoa and Scotland.

"It's a real test of our mental and physical preparation," admitted head coach Tandy.

"We can't assume that because one scoreboard went our way, everything is fixed.

"We have to double-down on performance, how we recover, how we train and executing the core areas of our game.

"We have to be at our absolute best to compete with the Aussies."

Tandy frequently talks about performance rather than results, yet this is an occasion where an ugly victory would do.

Wales' belief has soared but they remain slight underdogs for the fixture.

The odds are not as generous as last week's 20-1, but Tandy's men are hunting another scalp.

They are ninth in the world rankings and the Wallabies are seventh.

"It's not do or die, but they will want the performance and result," former Wales hooker Scott Baldwin told the Scrum V podcast.

"None of us expected the New Zealand win, it was one for the ages. If they perform anywhere near that then they win quite comfortably.

"After you have beaten the All Blacks, you go into the Six Nations believing you can beat anyone."

Wales enjoyed their moment, dealt with the acclaim, soaked in the social media reactions and fulfilled plenty of extra media requests.

But they were back in for training on Monday afternoon - business as usual(ish).

"I don't think anyone really felt a sore body until Tuesday because of the emotion and riding the weekend," said captain Dewi Lake.

"I have no doubt the boys will be ready to go.

"There might have been some things the coaches pulled here and there, some minutes off the clock, but the intensity, the challenge, the effort has been exactly the same.

"We've spoken about kicking on from this and to do that you just have to keep pushing."

Wales can go three from three in Cardiff and would then travel to London hunting a perfect November in a fixture likely to be against Japan.

Warren Gatland's class of 2018 are the only team to have enjoyed an autumn clean sweep.

Wales do not want to go from the biggest of highs against New Zealand - something that even the Grand Slam greats could not achieve - to a deflating home loss.

"When you come down off a high like that it is important you get the messaging right," said Gloucester hooker Lake.

"Steve, the coaches and other leaders have really delivered that this week in terms of it being an opportunity for us to build rather than it just being a one-off game we performed in that people will remember forever - but then we didn't turn up the week after.

"There are two ways we can go, we kick on or it's back to how we were. It's an opportunity to kick on."

The Wales players have had an extra day of recovery than the Wallabies, who lost to Scotland on Sunday, but Tandy's men did have a considerably bigger defensive effort and high ball-in-play time.

Wales used plenty of emotional and physical energy, leading to the management team freshening up their starting line-up.

They have gone back to the same XV that faced Japan a fortnight ago, and the pressure is on the returnees.

Blind-side flanker Alex Mann has been a favourite of Tandy's – starting in 12 of 14 Tests - but must now respond to Cardiff club-mate James Botham's excellence.

Lock Ben Carter got ahead of Adam Beard in the Six Nations but was tasked with providing energy off the bench last week.

The Dragons co-captain gets back in courtesy of Beard suffering a minor shoulder issue and must deliver when calling at the line-out after an off-day against Japan.

Wing Josh Adams, who was rested, and number eight Aaron Wainwright, back from a leg injury, have nothing to prove on the Test stage but would not be human if they were not a little disappointed to have missed out on making history.

Back row Taine Basham and wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb go from the starting line-up to missing out, with Kane James given the role of impact sub.

The promising Exeter flanker is set for a first international appearance in Cardiff after winning his first cap in Argentina in July.

"We have fresh and hungry players coming in, which will add the energy that we need," said Tandy.

Eleven Wales players are set for their third start on the spin, with the coaching staff poised to rotate for Twickenham.

An unfriendly kick-off time for the Wallabies fixture presented a challenge to the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU), but then Lake and his team ensured a ticket surge.

A crowd of 55,152 witnessed history against New Zealand at the 74,000-capacity Principality Stadium - but the 62,000 mark has already been passed for Australia.

"Our performance drives people to come and watch us and get behind us," said Lake.

"We saw that in spades last Saturday for every try and the defensive shifts. I think the loudest cheer was for a held-up ball or Eddie James and Louis Rees-Zammit's tackle [of a New Zealander] into touch in the 77th minute.

"That's what drives us on the field as well. The energy that we get from the crowd does help massively and our performance drives that, it's not shock that the two go hand in hand.

"We've seen how it's kind of given the nation a bit of hope. We've seen loads of videos rolling in, and that hope drives us as well."

A win against Australia would not prompt tears of joy in the stands, but Wales want to celebrate again after so much post-World Cup pain.

Wales will not mathematically know their Twickenham opponents before kick-off against the Wallabies, but they could be 99% certain to finish fifth.

If Scotland win with a bonus point against Japan then Tandy's side would need to do likewise, and win by 20 points more than the Scots.

Wales cannot drop to sixth and are likely to finish fifth, and that will mean another meeting with Japan unless Fiji win in Italy with a bonus point.

The Fijians would also need to turn around a hefty points difference gap to the Brave Blossoms.

The game between the fifth-placed teams is on Saturday, 28 November (13:10 GMT), followed in the double-header by the nations that finish second in the respective southern and northern tables.

articles.title: Scotland 67-5 Japan: Captain Stafford McDowall delighted with win
articles.text:
Stand-in captain Stafford McDowall praised Scotland for keeping their "foot on the throat" of opponents Japan in their thumping 67-5 Nations Championship win at Murrayfield.

After a disappointing defeat by New Zealand to start their autumn campaign, Gregor Townsend's side responded with a gritty victory against Australia last weekend and built on that performance against a depleted Japan outfit.

They led 29-0 at half-time, before going through the gears in the second half.

Eleven tries, including hat-tricks from winger Darcy Graham and effervescent young flanker Liam McConnell, boosted Scotland's chances of finishing third in the Northern Hemisphere table.

The Scots will likely face either Argentina or Australia in their competition finale next weekend, depending on results elsewhere on Saturday.

"We got off to a good start, which helped settle a few of the boys' nerves," said McDowall, who led the team in the absence of Sione Tuipulotu and Rory Darge.

"We had a chat on the pitch before we went in at half-time saying we didn't want to let the game fizzle out and I'm most proud of the fact we kept our foot on the throat in the second half. The boys that came off the bench did really well.

"I think it's a big step for this group and hopefully it's enough to bump us up the table. We are looking forward to the Six Nations and all those northern hemisphere teams are going to want to finish on a positive note."

While McConnell took the headlines for his try-scoring exploits, head coach Townsend was keen to highlight the work of the entire back row.

"Matt Fagerson went through a lot of work and hopefully his injury isn't serious. Ollie Leatherbarrow was great on both sides of the ball and Liam [McConnell] stands out for his tries."

Graham extended his lead as Scotland's record try scorer with his 39th, 40th and 41st international scores and, given the need to win handsomely in order to increase their points difference, Townsend was delighted with his team's execution.

"Japan were tough opposition. I know the scoreline doesn't suggest that, but it took a number of phases, really good focus at the breakdown, really smart decision-making to score in the first half," he said.

"The pressure told. The work we did in the first half not only got points on the board, but put pressure on Japan.

"Obviously we had an eye on that points total and getting to that number of points was an ambition and they delivered on that."

articles.title: Las Vegas Grand Prix: George Russell says 'somebody has to stand up to' Max Verstappen
articles.text:
The Las Vegas Grand Prix will start with two drivers on the front row who dislike each other - and after qualifying one said of the other that "somebody has got to stand up to that guy".

"That guy" is Max Verstappen, who starts his Red Bull from pole position. The driver criticising him is Mercedes' George Russell, who lines up second.

Both were promoted after the fastest qualifier, new world champion Kimi Antonelli, was demoted by a five-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine allocation for the season.

Russell's beef stemmed from an incident in final practice, in which Verstappen overtook the Mercedes on the Las Vegas Strip, then veered in front of him into Turn 14.

Russell, unhappy with the Dutchman's behaviour, dived down the Red Bull's inside on braking for the corner, got alongside, and then made his displeasure known by pushing Verstappen wide, the two cars making light contact.

They were called to the stewards to discuss the incident. Verstappen was given a warning having been found to have made an "unpredictable change of direction under braking".

After qualifying, Russell told Sky Italia: "I think the warning was fine. There's nothing in the rules to say that you cannot overtake someone who is starting their lap but when you do this, you are screwing this person over.

"He does this week in, week out, with many drivers. Everybody accepts it and I am not just going to accept somebody to screw me over like this and walk around like they are bigger and better than everyone else. Somebody has got to stand up to that guy."

Russell's comments were not put to Verstappen as he had finished his media commitments by the time they emerged into wider knowledge in Las Vegas.

Asked about the incident in the official news conference, Verstappen said: "Nothing happened."

When Verstappen spoke to the Dutch media, he was again reluctant to be drawn on it.

But asked whether it gave him extra motivation to beat Russell in the race, he said: "I don't need any extra motivation."

These two have history. This incident is almost exactly two years since they fell out in public following a row at the Qatar Grand Prix where Verstappen felt Russell had stepped over the line to get him a penalty that demoted him from pole position.

They exchanged insults. Russell, in remarks that echo those from Las Vegas, said: "People have been bullied by Max for years now."

Verstappen called Russell a "backstabber" and a "loser".

That was just the latest in a series of incidents - after a clash in Azerbaijan in 2022, Verstappen called Russell "Princess George" in a spat the Briton called "a little bit pathetic".

And then there was the 2025 Spanish Grand Prix. Late in the race, with Verstappen struggling with his tyres, they banged wheels as Russell attempted an overtake.

Verstappen retained the position after going off track and after being told by his team to hand the position to Russell, he moved over for the Mercedes and then appeared back on its inside and made contact with it.

He was penalised 10 seconds for that, and the following day issued a public apology for his behaviour.

All this certainly adds a hefty dose of extra spice to a race which, frankly, needs it.

This is the first of three 'dead rubbers' to close the season now both championships have been settled. There is little to fight for, and very little enthusiasm in the paddock for the final two races in the war-torn Middle East.

Despite widespread disquiet about going to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, everyone has been towing the party line on that one recently in public, that they trust governing body the FIA and Formula 1 to have made the right decision.

After qualifying, though, Verstappen came close to becoming the first to break the omerta, when he told the Dutch media "of course I would rather be at home", before repeating that he trusted the sport's bosses on the matter.

BBC Sport has been told of at least one other major driver who would rather not be going to the Middle East specifically because of concerns about safety.

As for the racing here in Sin City, it is set up beautifully.

The two drivers on the front row, as well as not troubling to hide their distaste for each other, are also the only two to have won here.

Verstappen has won two of the three events on the Strip circuit, sandwiching Russell's victory in 2024.

In theory, that could give an opportunity to McLaren's Lando Norris, who qualified fourth, and starts third as a result of Antonelli's penalty.

But the 2025 world champion was concerned about the McLaren's lack of straight-line speed.

"The pace in the car is not bad," he said. "The car is performing well, but our straight-line speed is so far off that we are not going to be able to overtake someone, so I think it's going to be a tough day."

His team principal Andrea Stella was more optimistic.

McLaren's battle with Red Bull for third in the constructors' championship - the two are separated by just 17 points - is one of the few major issues still to be settled this year.

Stella saw the fact that Norris had missed out on beating Russell by just 0.02secs, despite having a plastic bag caught in his floor that he said had cost 0.1secs, as reason for optimism.

As were the lessons of the Italian Grand Prix - held on a track with similarly long straights and big braking zones.

"We saw that because of this towing effect you actually can stay tangled, linked to the other cars," Stella said. "So we are definitely looking forward to tomorrow and encouraged by the fact that qualifying has been competitive.

"Because the tow effect is so big and because it's bigger than Monza, racing will be difficult to predict.

"So we need to make sure that from a driver's team point of view, we are ready for all the situations.

"It's also a circuit that may offer quite a few safety cars, and will be interesting, for instance, restarting from safety car with a tyre warm-up. Definitely an interesting one to be part of and to follow."

articles.title: England in Australia: Nikhil Chaudhary stars as hosts win T20 series opener
articles.text:
First T20, Melbourne Cricket Ground

England 187-9 (20 overs): Brook 65 (28), Banton 39 (22); Chaudhary 2-21

Australia 191-7 (19.5 overs): Chaudhary 66 (38)

Australia won by three wickets

Unlikely Australia international Nikhil Chaudhary rattled England and was the match-winner in a tense and tetchy final-over victory in the first T20 international in Melbourne.

Born in Delhi and a team-mate of India captain Shubman Gill in Indian domestic cricket, Chaudhary only switched to representing Australia after the Covid pandemic meant he got stuck in Brisbane celebrating his 24th birthday.

Progression through Australian club and domestic cricket followed - plus a stint working in a Mexican restaurant - before the 30-year-old played his standout performance to date in his fourth international at the Melbourne Cricket Ground.

Helping restrict England to 187-9 despite Harry Brook's fireworks in smashing 65 off 28 balls, Chaudhary took 2-21 with his mystery spin and then hit 66 to steer Australia within 20 runs of victory.

The elegant right-hander appeared to anger both Liam Dawson and Sam Curran during his knock and the MCG crowd loudly booed England as the tourists slowed the game in the final moments.

"You always know it is going to be a big game against England so there is going to be some chirp," said Chaudhary.

Curran was left with 11 to defend from the last over but all-rounder Jack Edwards finished with 25 not out as Australia completed their highest chase on home soil with three wickets and one ball remaining.

The win offers some relief to Australia - an XI featuring a host of new faces putting aside the ongoing sandpaper scandal to take a 1-0 lead in the five-match series.

England can level the contest in Gold Coast on Tuesday.

After all of the off-field issues that have overshadowed this tour, this was a welcome entertaining game of cricket.

England lost Phil Salt to the first ball of the match and afterwards there was boundary-hitting, comically bad fielding by Australia, a bit of needle and a grandstand finish.

Chaudhary should take the headlines. After opener Jake Fraser-McGurk fell in the first over and Mitchell Marsh was sluggish in making 37, he found scoring more straightforward.

He repeatedly targeted the off side and, after Australia lost 3-13 from 143-3, he pressed on the accelerator by hitting Will Jacks for six and Jamie Overton for two fours.

The incidents with Dawson and Curran appeared innocuous but words were exchanged. The umpire intervened in the Curran spat to encourage Chaudhary to continue his innings.

By hitting Overton to deep square-leg at the end of the 18th over, he allowed England back into the game.

However, Edwards kept his nerve, while England also had to deal with Jacks having to leave the field with a cut hand after four balls of the penultimate over.

Chaudhary once said he switched allegiance to Australia because he feels "more close to Australian culture than Indian culture".

Fittingly then, he experienced the wild cheers of an MCG crowd after the winning runs were hit.

"My parents came over from India last night," he said. "It is their first game watching me as well."

articles.title: Titans DL Jaylen Harrell hospitalized after car accident in Tampa
articles.text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- Tennessee Titans defensive lineman Jaylen Harrell was involved in a serious car accident Friday and remains hospitalized, according to the team.

Harrell, 24, was a passenger in an Uber in Tampa, Florida, when the accident occurred. No further details were available.

"Yesterday, Jaylen Harrell was involved in a serious car accident that resulted in him being taken to the hospital in his hometown of Tampa, Florida," the Titans said in a statement. "We have been in constant communication with Jaylen's family and are still working to gather more information.

"At this time, Jaylen remains in the hospital and continues to receive care. We ask that Jaylen and his family's privacy be respected at this time. We will provide an update when appropriate."

Harrell tore his ACL in the preseason and was placed on season-ending injured reserve. The Titans selected Harrell in the seventh round of the 2024 draft, and he finished his rookie season with 13 combined tackles.

He started two games for Tennessee in 2025 and 25 combined tackles, including 4.5 sacks and a forced fumble.

articles.title: Sources: Texas A&M expected to bench Marcel Reed, start Brady Hart
articles.text:
Texas A&M is expected to make a change at quarterback Saturday, going with Brady Hart over Marcel Reed against Oklahoma, sources confirmed to ESPN.

Hart, a sophomore, has thrown for 165 yards in limited action over four games this season, including last week when he replaced Reed in the Aggies' loss to Tennessee. He has two touchdowns and two interceptions.

He gets his first start against the Sooners, who have the fifth-best defense in the SEC, allowing 294.6 yards per game.

Reed has struggled throughout the season as the Aggies, who were No. 8 in the preseason AP Top 25 poll after reaching the College Football Playoff last season, are 1-6 in SEC play (4-6 overall) while ranking 13th in the conference in total offense.

"Our offense is inept," coach Mike Elko told reporters earlier this week. "I don't know how you could put this on one kid. ... It's on me. It is on me. It is a completely nonfunctional offense, and it is on me."

The dual-threat Reed has thrown for 1,712 yards while completing a career-low 55.7% of his passes with eight touchdowns and nine interceptions. The senior has 206 rushing yards with three touchdowns.

In four seasons with the Aggies, Reed has thrown for 7,119 yards with 66 combined touchdowns and 28 interceptions. He has rushed for 1,291 yards.
